# Wholemeal Sourdough

## Overview

The trick that makes this loaf work is that the bran is soaked with the mixing water in a 30-minute soaker before anything else goes in, so it softens and stops tearing the gluten when the dough is worked. Wholemeal flour carries sharp flecks of bran that act like tiny blades, slicing through the gluten strands as the dough is folded, and a dry soaker avoids that entirely. I let the flour and water sit together for half an hour, then add the starter and salt, and the dough behaves almost like a strong white loaf from there. I use 40% wholemeal against 60% strong white flour at a 78% hydration mix. Wholemeal alone gives a dense, dry crumb, and white flour gives it the lift and the open texture that make it worth baking. The result is nutty and substantial without being heavy, and it toasts to a deep gold. The soaker is the single change that lifted this loaf from a brick to something I make every week, and it costs nothing but patience. I bake mine in a covered pot on a hot stone and it comes out with a chewy crust and a soft, even crumb every time. It is the loaf I make most often in winter, when a dense slice with butter and a bowl of soup is exactly what the day calls for.

## Method

I start with the soaker, which means the wholemeal flour and the mixing water go into the bowl together thirty minutes before anything else. I weigh 200 g of wholemeal flour into a large bowl and pour over 390 g of water, stir it into a rough porridge, and cover it while I get the rest of the kit out. That half hour is the whole point: the water reaches the bran and softens it, and by the time the dough forms, those flakes can no longer cut the gluten.

After the soaker has sat, I add 300 g of strong white flour, 200 g of active starter, and 10 g of salt, then mix everything with a dough hook for four minutes until it forms a shaggy, sticky dough. The hydration sits at 78% and the dough will feel wetter than a white loaf, which is normal.

I bulk ferment it for four hours at room temperature and give it three folds spaced about forty minutes apart, wetting my hand each time and stretching the dough up and over itself from four sides. Wholemeal dough is easy to tear, so the folds stay gentle.

I shape it into a boule and cold proof it overnight in the fridge. In the morning I heat the oven and a covered pot to 235 C, turn the loaf out, score it, and bake it covered for 20 minutes at 235 C, then uncover it and finish at 220 C for 25 minutes until the crust is deep brown and the base sounds hollow. I let the loaf cool on a wire rack for at least an hour, and I resist cutting it while it is still warm because the crumb needs that time to set. The loaf should sound hollow when I tap the base, and the internal temperature should read above 96 C, which tells me the middle is cooked through.

## Notes

Wholemeal flour is thirsty, and the bran holds water that the gluten cannot use, so the mash and the mix have to be judged by feel rather than by the scale alone. If the dough feels stiff after the soaker, a spoonful of water brings it back; too dry and the loaf bakes up tight and crumbly. I sift nothing out of the flour, because the bran is the flavour and the soak has already neutralised its worst behaviour. The three folds in the bulk are there to build a little tension without the strain a long knead would put on the wholemeal gluten. I keep the covered stage at 235 C because I want the crust set before the sugars in the bran have a chance to scorch, and the cooler uncovered finish dries the loaf out evenly. Cool it on a rack for at least an hour, because cutting a warm wholemeal loaf smears the crumb. It keeps two days in a paper bag and slices best on the second day. If the loaf browns too fast on top, a sheet of foil laid loosely over it for the last ten minutes saves the crust, and the bread still finishes cooking through. I have baked this with a little honey in the soaker when I wanted a sweeter loaf, and it worked well, though I usually leave it out because the wholemeal already carries enough flavour of its own.
